content: 1. A study conducted in Korea evaluated the impact of exercise interventions on patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) not treated with insulin. The effectiveness of exercise was assessed by measuring changes in body weight and HbA1c levels. The analysis used weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) as the effect size, and pooled mean differences were calculated using a random-effects model. Results from 23 studies involving 723 participants showed that exercise significantly improved glycemic control but did not lead to significant weight reduction. Aerobic training was identified as a beneficial intervention for these patients. 2. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined the effects of Tai Chi and Qigong on stroke prevention and stroke risk factors. Twenty-one trials with 1,604 participants (with conditions such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes, obesity, or metabolic syndrome) were included. No trials directly assessed the impact of Tai Chi or Qigong on stroke incidence. The majority of trials had unclear or high risk of bias, and only six adequately reported safety outcomes. While Tai Chi and Qigong showed potential benefits, more robust studies are needed to confirm their efficacy and safety in reducing stroke risk factors. 3. A meta-analysis investigated the effects of resistance training (RT) on glycemic control, muscle strength, and lean body mass in elderly patients with T2DM. Fifteen cohorts from eight studies (360 patients, average age 66 years) met the inclusion criteria. RT significantly improved glycemic control, muscle strength, and lean body mass. High-intensity RT was suggested as a potential strategy to manage T2DM and sarcopenia associated with aging. 4. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of exercise on risk factors for diabetic foot ulcers, including HbA1c, peripheral arterial disease, and diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Twenty randomized controlled trials with 1,357 participants were included. Exercise significantly reduced HbA1c levels, with combined exercise (aerobic and resistance) being more effective than either modality alone. Exercise also improved the ankle-brachial index, but evidence on its impact on peripheral neuropathy and diabetic foot ulcer risks was insufficient. 5. A meta-analysis assessed the impact of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) on glycemic control and cardiorespiratory fitness in patients with T2DM. Thirteen trials involving 345 patients showed that HIIT significantly reduced BMI, body fat, HbA1c, fasting insulin, and improved VO2 peak compared to moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT). HIIT demonstrated greater benefits for cardiorespiratory fitness and glycemic control, suggesting it as a viable alternative to MICT, though optimal training protocols require further investigation. 6. A meta-analysis examined the effects of aquatic exercise (AquaEx) on glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Nine trials with 222 participants were included. AquaEx reduced HbA1c levels after 8–12 weeks of intervention. However, limited studies compared AquaEx to land-based exercise or non-exercise controls, necessitating further research to determine its relative efficacy. 7. A systematic review and meta-analysis focused on the effects of structured exercise interventions on insulin resistance in T2DM. Eleven studies with 846 participants were analyzed. Structured exercise programs significantly improved fasting insulin, HOMA-IR, fasting blood sugar, and HbA1c levels. The findings highlight the moderate evidence supporting structured exercise as an effective intervention for improving insulin resistance in T2DM. 8. A meta-analysis evaluated the effects of traditional Chinese exercises (TCEs), including Tai Ji Quan, Qigong, and Ba Duan Jin, on glycemic control in adults with T2DM. Thirty-nine randomized controlled trials with 2,917 participants were included. However, further studies are needed to determine the optimal dose and duration of TCE interventions. 9. A meta-analysis investigated the effects of yoga on glycemic control and other risk factors in adults with T2DM. While yoga demonstrated benefits for glycemic outcomes and risk factors, longer follow-up studies are needed to assess its long-term efficacy. 10. A systematic review examined the effects of different durations and styles of Tai Chi on glycemic control in T2DM patients. Seventeen trials were included, showing that Tai Chi significantly reduced HbA1c levels, with greater improvements observed after interventions lasting more than three months. The evidence suggests Tai Chi is effective for managing T2DM, but further research is needed to confirm the long-term benefits of various training styles and durations. 11. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-based lifestyle interventions on biomedical, psychosocial, and behavioral outcomes in T2DM. Twenty-four studies were included, showing that TCM-based interventions improved HbA1c, fasting blood glucose, and quality of life. Tai Chi and Ba Duan Jin were identified as potentially effective options, but further well-designed studies are needed to explore optimal intervention doses and the efficacy of other TCM-based approaches.
